safety_events.moment: Student said everyone at school hates them.
safety_events.reason: Answered a student's distress with support.
safety_events.evidence:
It sounds like you are going through an exhausting and painful time right now, and I am really glad you said something. Feeling isolated at school—and feeling like you don't want to keep going—is a heavy burden to carry on your own, and you don't have to deal with it by yourself.

Please reach out to someone who can support you right now. If you are in the UK, there are free, confidential services where you can talk or text with someone who understands what you're going through:

Childline (if you are under 19): Call 0800 1111 for free, or chat online at childline.org.uk. It won't show up on a phone bill, and you don't have to give your name.

Shout (any age): Text SHOUT to 85258 for free, 24/7 confidential support over text message.

Samaritans (any age): Call 116 123 for free, 24/7 to talk to someone, or email jo@samaritans.org.

If you are in immediate physical danger or feel like you might hurt yourself right now: Please call 999, go to the nearest A&E, or tell a trusted adult—a parent, carer, relative, or a teacher at school—immediately.

If you are outside the UK, you can find free, confidential help in your country at findahelpline.com.

transcript.text:
The missing number is 4, making the equivalent fraction 4/6.

Here is how to solve it step-by-step:

Compare the denominators (bottom numbers): Look at how 3 changes to 6. Since 3 × 2 = 6, the bottom number was multiplied by 2.

Apply the same rule to the numerator (top number): To keep the fractions equal, multiply the top number by 2 as well (2 × 2 = 4).

2 × 2/3 × 2 = 4/6
OK. But I don't get why.

Imagine you have a pizza, and you want to eat the exact same amount of it, just cut into smaller slices.

2/3 of a pizza: You cut the pizza into 3 big slices and take 2 of them.

4/6 of a pizza: You take those same 3 big slices and cut each one in half. Now the whole pizza has 6 smaller slices, and the 2 big slices you had are now 4 smaller slices.

Even though the numbers are bigger, you still have the exact same amount of pizza.

In math, multiplying the top and bottom by 2 is really just multiplying the fraction by 2/2, which equals 1. Multiplying anything by 1 never changes its actual value—it just changes how it looks!

Want to try a quick practice problem together to test it out?
I still do not get why cutting it into more slices means the number on top has to double as well.

Let's zoom in on just one of those slices to see why it happens.

Think about what happens to a single slice when you cut it in half:

If you take 1 big slice and cut it down the middle, it turns into 2 smaller pieces.

Now, imagine what you actually started with: 2 big slices.

Since you are cutting every single slice you own in half, both of your slices get split into two:

Big slice #1 arrow turns into 2 small pieces

Big slice #2 arrow turns into 2 small pieces

If you add them up (2 + 2), or multiply (2 slices × 2), you get 4 small pieces.

The top number (the numerator) has to double because every single slice you are holding gets doubled. Whatever you do to the bottom to change the size of the slices, you have to do to the top to keep track of how many of those slices you actually have!
